title: the saint who wrote about prayer like a friendship
hookLine: the saint who wrote about prayer like a friendship
carry: talk to him like a friend

cards: Sit down to pray, or just to be quiet, and within a minute the mind has gone to lunch, or an argument from last week, or whether the car is locked.

A woman in Spain, long ago, admitted in writing that for years prayer went like that for her. She would listen for the clock to strike, wishing the hour were over. She was a nun, and prayer was her whole job.
Later the Church would call her a teacher of prayer for everyone.

teach.b: Her name was Teresa, from the walled city of Ávila in Spain.

She grew up in a big, lively family, and as a girl, by her own account, she cared more for books of knights and adventure, and for nice clothes, than for holiness. As a young woman she entered a Carmelite convent.
And for years, she says in her autobiography, prayer was a struggle. Distracted, dry, going through the motions.
Then, after a long time, something changed, and the way she described prayer afterward is the reason she's still read.
Prayer, as she understands it, is nothing else than friendship: spending time often, alone, with the one we know loves us. Not a performance. Not a speech.
Time with a friend. She wrote the way she talked: funny, blunt, full of kitchen pictures. She said God walks among the pots and pans.
In another book, she pictures the soul as a castle made of a single diamond, with many rooms, and God living in the center. Prayer is the door you go in by. She also got a lot done.
She founded new convents across Spain, traveling on bad roads in rough carts, arguing with bishops, and working with a young friar we know as John of the Cross.

There's a story people love to tell: that after a cart tipped her into a muddy river, she complained to God, if this is how you treat your friends, no wonder you have so few. Nobody knows whether she really said it.

teach.h: TALK TO HIM LIKE A FRIEND.
teach.b: But it sounds exactly like someone who talked to God like a friend. Long after her death, the Church named her a Doctor of the Church: a teacher for everyone.

how: Catholics keep a feast day for Saint Teresa of Ávila each year; her books on prayer, especially her Life and The Interior Castle, are still read, and Carmelite nuns and friars follow the reform she began.

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: what she listened for during dry prayer
the soul, with God at the center
the young friar she worked with

s: Teresa found prayer easy from the start
she wrote that for years it was dry and distracted, and she listened for the clock to strike.
she said God walks among the pots and pans
one of her kitchen pictures: God is found in ordinary work too.
historians have confirmed she said "no wonder you have so few friends"
it's a story people love to tell. nobody knows if she said it.

games.q: you're a nun in Teresa's Spain, and after years, prayer still feels dry. how does Teresa end up describing prayer?
o: as friendship: time alone with the one who loves you.
as something only for the very holy.
games.why: her autobiography calls prayer nothing else than friendship, time often spent alone with the one we know loves us.

practice: Here's the practice, with no speech to give. Imagine a friend sitting across from you, one who knows you well and likes you anyway. Tell them, silently, one plain thing about your day.
Not the polished version. Then just sit together without talking. When your mind wanders, and it will, come back the way you'd turn back to a friend after a distraction.
If you pray, you can make that friend God.

wordCard.voice: Teresa of Ávila. The Carmelite nun who struggled with prayer for years, then described it as friendship with the one who loves us. Twentieth word.

orig.note: Teresa's own Spanish, not Latin: to spend time as friends. her phrase for prayer, in her Life, chapter 8.

carryVoice: Your line: talk to him like a friend. No speech, no polish: just time together. Day twenty.
